subtitle: The first guide to the early Network Working Group notes: nine categories, what is current, and what to read first.

tldr.problem: By February 1971 the NWG/RFC series numbered 102 notes, and it was hard to tell which were current, obsolete or superseded.
tldr.mechanism: P. Karp of MITRE sorts the notes into 9 categories (A to I) with subcategories, summarises each, and marks a minimum subset worth reading to learn the current status.
tldr.outcome: This initial Guide was issued as an RFC to collect comments for about two weeks, ahead of an official version planned for March 26 as a separate series of documents.

today: The metadata gives this RFC an Unknown status and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a February 1971 snapshot, and the text says an official version was planned for March 26.

sections.title: Why a Guide to the Notes
sections.content:
The NWG/RFC Guide tries to bring order to the series, which now numbers 102. It categorizes the notes, identifies the topics under discussion and the relevant RFCs, and says whether each note is current, obsolete or superseded.

A minimum subset is identified: the notes one should read to quickly become familiar with the current status of topics. For readers tracing a topic's development, a brief summary is given for each relevant note.

Karp invites comments for about two weeks and admits he has not had to implement an NCP and may have misconceptions about technical points. He also prefers to keep the sequential numbering, since numbers like #33, #66 and #83 serve as shorthand in meetings.
sections.eli5: There were too many notes to keep track of. This guide says which are still useful and which are old news.

sections.title: The Nine Categories
sections.content:
For each category, the Guide names the official document (if any), the unresolved issues and the documents still to be published. Host/IMP (Level 1) rests on BBN Memo No. 1822, and Host/Host (Level 2) on Document No. 1 by S. Crocker, 3 August 1970, as modified by RFC 102. The Host/Host topics include connection establishment, flow control, interrupt handling, error control and dynamic reconnection, and the software that implements them is the Network Control Program (NCP).

Subsystem Level (Level 3) has no official document and all issues are unresolved. Three committees were set up for the logger, console and TELNET protocols, for data transformation, and for graphics. The guide notes that most of the current subset addresses this category.
sections.eli5: The folders are labelled things like Administrative, Host/IMP, Host/Host, Measurement and Accounting, so you can find a note by topic.

sections.title: Current Notes and Open Items
sections.content:
The subset reflecting current status is NWG/RFC numbers 5, 12, 30-33, 41, 47, 48, 51, 53-56, 60, 62, 66, 74, 76-78, 80-83, 86-91, 94-100 and 102. The Guide then lists the notes by number with the relevant categories.

Other pieces were promised: a meeting report by Dick Watson of SRI on the University of Illinois meeting, a Document No. 2 by S. Crocker, an accounting RFC by B. Kahn of BBN, and documentation procedures from Watson. The guide also calls for notes on network experience, reporting for example NCP checkout between UCSB and RAND in RFC 78.
sections.eli5: The guide gives a short reading list and a to-do list of notes that people had promised to write.

items.desc: Distribution list, meeting notices and minutes, policies.

items.desc: Official document: Document No. 1, with RFC 102 changes.

items.label: Subsystem Level Protocol (Level 3)
items.desc: Logger, console, TELNET, graphics and file transmission; no official document.

items.desc: Reports on early use of the network.

items.desc: Procedures for entering documentation at the NIC.
